subject: Measurement Invariance; Constraint Loadings lead to increase in number of parameters

messages.author: 577ea47fb96b25a9
messages.subject: Measurement Invariance; Constraint Loadings lead to increase in number of parameters
parts:
Dear all,

I am fairly new to using lavaan (and SEM, too), and just searched for 2 hours to see whether I can find a helpful answer - I might be asking something obvious, and if I missed a matching thread, excuse the following.

I am running a SEM analysis with group comparison for gender. The model is quite simple:

PandModel <-'
  StresVS  =~ bw.4.t1r + bw.5.t1r + bw.2.t1r +  bw.3.t1r + bw.6.t1r 
  StresLS  =~ bs.4.t1r + bs.5.t1r + bs.1.t1r
  StresRSA =~ bl.3.t1r + bl.1.t1r + bl.4.t1r
  StresRSC =~ bc.2.t1r + bc.3.t1r + bc.1.t1r + bc.4.t1r 

  CUS      =~ a*co.17.t1 + a*co.24.t1

  CUS ~ StresVS + StresLS + StresRSA + StresRSC + ac.neg.b.t1 + ac.abus.b.t1
'

In order to check measurement invariance I compared the Free Model to a loading-constraint model:

ModelFitG.1 <- sem(PandModel, data = dat, std.lv=T, estimator="DWLS", se="robust", test = "Satorra.Bentler",  group = "s.genf.t1")

# Constrain Loadings (check Measurement Invariance)
ModelFitG.2 <- sem(PandModel, data = dat, std.lv=T, estimator="DWLS", se="robust", test = "Satorra.Bentler", group = "s.genf.t1", group.equal = c("loadings"))

All works well, no errors and there is no significant difference between groups.

But when comparing the two, I found that instead of an additional 15 df (15 constraint loadings), I only get +10. So I looked into my output and found, that for the ModelFitG.2 I have an additional 5 parameters to be estimated, too. I checked the free parameters using lavInspect(ModelFit**, "free") and when comparing the two Models, found that $`Male`$psi differs as follows:

ModelFitG.1

$`Male`$psi

         StrsVS StrsLS StrRSA StrRSC CUS

StresVS    0                            

StresLS  110      0                     

StresRSA 111    113   0              

StresRSC 112    114  115     0      

CUS       0      0    0      0      0 

  

ModelFitG.2

$`Male`$psi

               StrsVS StrsLS StrRSA StrRSC CUS

StresVS  110                            

StresLS  115     111                     

StresRSA 116     118    112              

StresRSC 117     119    120   113      

 CUS      0       0      0     0     114


And here's where I don't understand (or maybe don't interpret correctly):
It appears that the variances/covariances of the latent variables is completely
 free only for the constraint-loading model and only for the 2nd Group in the comparison. 

Why is this - and do I have to do anything about it? Any help, comment, or tip is much appreciated!


[ Additional Info: I did run my analysis without the "std.lv=T" call previously and didn't run into this change in parameters ]


Thank you 
Tabea

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Measurement Invariance; Constraint Loadings lead to increase in number of parameters
parts: instead of an additional 15 df (15 constraint loadings), I only get +10

Right, because you need to free the 5 factor variances in Group 2.  When loadings are constrained to equality, fixing factor variances to 1 in *both* groups is not necessary for identification.  If you left them fixed, you would be testing equivalence of loadings *and* variances.  When std.lv=FALSE, the variances are free in both groups already, and you only constrain 10 loadings because 5 reference indicators have loadings fixed to 1.  But those are statistically equivalent parameterizations for continuous data (you can even mix/match when comparing configural to metric invariance).

However, you are requesting DWLS, which is designed specifically for categorical data (i.e., the weight matrix contains sampling variances of threshold and polychoric-correlation estimates).  Yet you aren't declaring any variables as categorical---perhaps they are already of class c("ordered","factor") in the data.frame dat?  

If they are ordinal, then you cannot meaningfully compare factor loadings across groups unless thresholds are constrained across groups.  Constraining thresholds links the response scales across groups, so you can actually test whether a 1-unit increase in the factor corresponds to the same expected increase (in the same units) of the latent response underlying the categorical indicator.  

https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-016-9506-0

https://doi.org/10.1007/s11136-018-1785-8

https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1602776
